title: Does LinUCB Need Valid Confidence Sets?

paper.title: Does LinUCB Need Valid Confidence Sets?
paper.abstract: Abstract We show that replacing LinUCB’s usual confidence width β \beta by any fixed α > 0 \alpha>0 preserves sublinear regret when the action set is M M -smooth and m m -strongly convex. Our high-probability regret bound for this generalisation, α \alpha -LinUCB, establishes that valid confidence sets are not necessary for the success of LinUCB. We identify the mechanism behind this result: action-set curvature drives α \alpha -LinUCB to explore every direction, even when optimism is not guaranteed. To analyse this mechanism, we introduce a logarithmically capped spectral potential that, unlike the standard log-determinant potential, caps contributions from well-explored directions. This yields lower bounds on the smallest eigenvalue of the design matrix. At the standard confidence width α = β ≍ d ​ log ⁡ T \alpha=\beta\asymp\sqrt{d\log T} , our T T -round regret bound in d d dimensions is 𝒪 ⁡ ( M m ​ d ​ T ​ log ⁡ T ) \mathcal{O}\bigl(\frac{M}{m}d\sqrt{T\log T}\bigr) , up to iterated-logarithmic factors, improving the horizon dependence of the classical LinUCB guarantee by a factor of log ⁡ T \sqrt{\log T} .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: A learner interacting with a bandit environment chooses actions sequentially to earn rewards while gathering the information needed to improve future decisions. We consider this exploration–exploitation trade-off in the stochastic linear bandit setting. Fix an unknown parameter θ ⋆ ∈ ℝ d \theta^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , a closed action set 𝒳 \mathcal{X} contained in the unit ball of ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} , and an integer horizon T ≥ 1 T\geq 1 . At each round t ∈ { 1 , … , T } t\in\{1,\dots,T\} , the learner selects an action x t ∈ 𝒳 x_{t}\in\mathcal{X} and receives a reward y t = ⟨ θ ⋆ , x t ⟩ + η t y_{t}={\langle\theta^{\star},x_{t}\rangle}+\eta_{t} , where the noise η t \eta_{t} is conditionally centred and sub-Gaussian. We consider the T T -round (pseudo-)regret, ℛ T := ∑ t = 1 T ⟨ θ ⋆ , x ⋆ − x t ⟩ , x ⋆ ∈ arg ​ max x ∈ 𝒳 ⁡ ⟨ θ ⋆ , x ⟩ . \mathcal{R}_{T}:=\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\langle\theta^{\star},x^{\star}-x_{t}\rangle},\qquad x^{\star}\in\argmax_{x\in\mathcal{X}}{\langle\theta^{\star},x\rangle}. LinUCB addresses this trade-off using upper confidence bounds on rewards ( Dani et al., 2008 ; Li et al., 2010 ; Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2011 ) . We study α \alpha -LinUCB ( Algorithm 1 ), a generalisation that treats the confidence width as a free parameter. Given fixed α , λ 0 > 0 \alpha,\lambda_{0}>0 , at each round t t , the algorithm selects x t x_{t} through ( x t , θ t ) ∈ arg ​ max ( x , θ ) ∈ 𝒳 × 𝒞 t ​ ( α ) ⁡ ⟨ θ , x ⟩ , 𝒞 t ​ ( α ) := { θ ∈ ℝ d : ∥ θ − θ ^ t ∥ V t ≤ α } , (x_{t},\theta_{t})\in\argmax_{(x,\theta)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{C}_{t}(\alpha)}{\langle\theta,x\rangle},\qquad\mathcal{C}_{t}(\alpha):=\left\{\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\lVert\theta-\hat{\theta}_{t}\rVert_{V_{t}}\leq\alpha\right\}, where θ ^ t = V t − 1 ​ ∑ s = 1 t − 1 x s ​ y s \hat{\theta}_{t}=V_{t}^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}x_{s}y_{s} is the ridge estimate of θ ⋆ \theta^{\star} with design V t := λ 0 ​ 𝐈 + ∑ s = 1 t − 1 x s ​ x s ⊤ V_{t}:=\lambda_{0}\mathbf{I}+\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}x_{s}x_{s}^{\top} . Equivalently, the action satisfies x t ∈ arg ​ max x ∈ 𝒳 ⁡ { ⟨ θ ^ t , x ⟩ + α ​ ∥ x ∥ V t − 1 } . x_{t}\in\argmax_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\left\{{\langle\hat{\theta}_{t},x\rangle}+\alpha\lVert x\rVert_{V_{t}^{-1}}\right\}. Thus, actions are selected through a combination of the mean and an α \alpha -weighted exploration bonus, with ∥ x ∥ V t − 1 \lVert x\rVert_{V_{t}^{-1}} being large for x x aligned with directions poorly represented by previous actions. Standard LinUCB chooses a confidence width β ≍ d ​ log ⁡ T \beta\asymp\sqrt{d\log T} so that θ ⋆ ∈ ⋂ t = 1 T 𝒞 t ​ ( β ) \theta^{\star}\in\bigcap_{t=1}^{T}\mathcal{C}_{t}(\beta) with high probability. On this event, the selected pair ( x t , θ t ) (x_{t},\theta_{t}) satisfies the optimism inequality ⟨ θ t , x t ⟩ ≥ ⟨ θ ⋆ , x ⋆ ⟩ {\langle\theta_{t},x_{t}\rangle}\geq{\langle\theta^{\star},x^{\star}\rangle} , which underlies its usual regret guarantee ( Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2011 ) . For arbitrary α > 0 \alpha>0 , α \alpha -LinUCB retains an exploration bonus, but its ellipsoids need not be valid confidence sets. The optimism inequality is then no longer guaranteed, so the usual regret argument does not extend to arbitrary choices of α \alpha . This raises the question: Does LinUCB Need Valid Confidence Sets? Under an additional curvature condition on the action set, we answer this question in the negative: • Regret without valid confidence sets. When the squared support function of the action set is M M -smooth and m m -strongly convex, we prove a high-probability regret bound of 1 1 1 Throughout, we use the standard asymptotic notation 𝒪 ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{O}(\cdot) and Ω ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \Omega(\cdot) , up to iterated-logarithm factors. ℛ T = 𝒪 ⁡ ( M m ​ α 2 + β 2 α ​ d ​ T ) , \mathcal{R}_{T}=\mathcal{O}\Bigl(\frac{M}{m}\frac{\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}}{\alpha}\sqrt{dT}\Bigr), up to iterated-logarithmic factors ( Theorem 4.2 ). The bound is sublinear for every fixed α > 0 \alpha>0 , including widths for which the exploration ellipsoids are not valid confidence sets. The geometric condition, stated in Assumption (A2) , includes Euclidean balls, ellipsoids, and convex bodies with uniformly positive and bounded curvature. • A geometric exploration mechanism. We identify the mechanism through which α \alpha -LinUCB works without optimism: action-set curvature drives α \alpha -LinUCB to explore every direction, even when optimism is not guaranteed. Our spectral theorem makes this precise by controlling the growth of the design matrix ( Theorem 4.3 ). On the unit ball, it gives a lower bound proportional to t \sqrt{t} on λ min ​ ( V t ) \lambda_{\min}(V_{t}) , holding with high probability at every round after a burn-in period; the general result controls the corresponding width in the action set geometry. • A logarithmically capped potential. To analyse this exploration mechanism, we introduce a logarithmically capped spectral potential that, unlike the standard log-determinant potential, caps contributions from well-explored directions. The resulting spectral bounds yield regret control without the usual elliptical-potential argument. At the standard width α = β \alpha=\beta , this gives 𝒪 ⁡ ( M m ​ d ​ T ​ log ⁡ T ) \mathcal{O}\bigl(\frac{M}{m}d\sqrt{T\log T}\bigr) regret, improving the horizon dependence of the classical 𝒪 ⁡ ( d ​ T ​ log ⁡ T ) \mathcal{O}(d\sqrt{T}\log T) guarantee by a factor of log ⁡ T \sqrt{\log T} , up to iterated-logarithmic factors. Moreover, we construct a counterexample confirming that assumptions on the action set are necessary: on a two-dimensional polygon, α \alpha -LinUCB incurs linear regret with constant probability, for every sufficiently small α > 0 \alpha>0 ( Proposition 6.1 ). We support our theoretical findings with experiments: on the unit ball, the observed regret and smallest-eigenvalue growth are consistent with the predicted t \sqrt{t} rates, even when the ellipsoids exclude the true parameter in most rounds.

sections.heading: 2 Related work
sections.text: Our work is closest to that of Abeille et al. (2025) , who use the same geometric condition to analyse Thompson sampling without forced optimism or posterior inflation. Banerjee et al. (2023) also connect curvature with exploration, deriving growth of the smallest eigenvalue of the expected design matrix from an assumed 𝒪 ⁡ ( T ) \mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T}) regret guarantee. We discuss these and further connections below.

sections.heading: Optimism and confidence sets in linear bandits.
sections.text: The classical 𝒪 ⁡ ( d ​ T ​ log ⁡ ( T ) ) \mathcal{O}(d\sqrt{T}\log\left(T\right)) regret analysis of LinUCB/OFUL combines self-normalised concentration with the elliptical-potential lemma ( Li et al., 2010 ; Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2011 ) . Each contributes a log ⁡ ( T ) \sqrt{\log\left(T\right)} factor, leaving a logarithmic gap to the Ω ⁡ ( d ​ T ) \Omega(d\sqrt{T}) minimax lower bound ( Dani et al., 2008 ; Rusmevichientong & Tsitsiklis, 2010 ; Lattimore & Szepesvári, 2020 ) . Lattimore (2023) proves that the continuous-time counterpart of the self-normalised concentration bound cannot be improved for general adaptive covariates. Flynn et al. (2023) construct tighter confidence sequences using adaptive martingale mixtures, improving empirical performance while retaining 𝒪 ⁡ ( d ​ T ​ log ⁡ ( T ) ) \mathcal{O}(d\sqrt{T}\log\left(T\right)) worst-case regret. Our analysis uses the standard confidence bound but with a logarithmically capped potential. Classical frequentist analyses of linear Thompson sampling also rely on optimism: posterior inflation ensures a constant probability of an optimistic draw, at the cost of an additional d \sqrt{d} factor in the regret bound ( Agrawal & Goyal, 2013 ; Abeille & Lazaric, 2017 ) . For finite-armed linear bandits, Lattimore & Szepesvári (2017) show that standard optimism-based algorithms can be suboptimal. Subsequent asymptotically optimal algorithms explicitly optimise exploration allocations to account for the information provided by suboptimal actions ( Hao et al., 2020 ; Tirinzoni et al., 2020 ) .

sections.heading: Action-set curvature and exploration.
sections.text: When the action set is smooth and strongly convex, the played arm x t = ∇ J 𝒳 ​ ( θ t ) x_{t}=\nabla J_{\mathcal{X}}(\theta_{t}) moves continuously with the parameter, and perturbations of the estimate translate into exploration. The benefit of curvature is classical in online learning, where follow-the-leader enjoys fast rates on strongly convex constraint sets for much the same reason ( Huang et al., 2016 ) . In stochastic bandits, Banerjee et al. (2023) quantify this: for action sets with bounded curvature around the optimal arm, any algorithm with 𝒪 ⁡ ( T ) \mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T}) expected regret has a design matrix whose minimum eigenvalue grows as Ω ⁡ ( T ) \Omega(\sqrt{T}) in expectation; in contrast well-separated arms ( Lattimore & Szepesvári, 2017 ) force eventual logarithmic growth. Abeille et al. (2025) exploit the same geometry, under the assumption we adopt here, to analyse randomised exploration without forced optimism or posterior inflation, and show that Thompson sampling attains 𝒪 ⁡ ( d ​ T ​ log ⁡ ( T ) ) \mathcal{O}(d\sqrt{T}\log\left(T\right)) regret. Taking α = 0 \alpha=0 in our decision rule gives the greedy policy. Greedy methods are studied in contextual bandits, but only known to succeed under diversity of contexts, either assumed ( Bastani et al., 2021 ) or induced by smoothing ( Kannan et al., 2018 ; Raghavan et al., 2023 ) . On a fixed action set no such diversity is available and, accordingly, our bound degrades as α → 0 \alpha\to 0 .

sections.heading: Inference under adaptive sampling.
sections.text: Conditions on the growth of the design matrix play a central role in inference from adaptively collected data, beginning with Lai & Wei (1982) . Ordinary least squares can have non-Gaussian asymptotic distributions and inflated estimation error under adaptive designs ( Khamaru et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2023 ) , motivating debiasing procedures that recover asymptotic normality under conditions on the data-collection process ( Deshpande et al., 2018 ; Khamaru et al., 2025 ; Ying et al., 2023 ; Lin et al., 2023 ) . A complementary approach establishes stability of the design after deterministic normalisation; Praharaj & Khamaru (2026) use this to obtain asymptotically valid Wald intervals for a regularised EXP4 algorithm in linear contextual bandits.

sections.heading: 4 Main Results
sections.text: We now present our regret upper bound for α \alpha -LinUCB. Its statement uses the standard concentration width β \beta and the concentration event ℰ \mathcal{E} of Abbasi-Yadkori et al. (2011) , which we first reproduce. Proposition 4.1 (Confidence event; Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2011 ) . Let Assumption (A1) hold, let ∥ θ ⋆ ∥ 2 ≤ S ⋆ \lVert\theta^{\star}\rVert_{2}\leq S^{\star} and 𝒳 ⊆ 𝔹 2 d ​ ( 1 ) \mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{B}_{2}^{d}(1) , and let θ ^ t \hat{\theta}_{t} be the ridge estimate with regularisation λ 0 > 0 \lambda_{0}>0 . Fix a horizon T T and a confidence level δ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \delta\in(0,1) , and define β : \displaystyle\beta\;: = μ ​ 2 ​ log ⁡ ( 1 δ ) + d ​ log ⁡ ( ( 1 + T d ​ λ 0 ) ) + λ 0 ​ S ⋆ , \displaystyle=\;\mu\sqrt{2\log\left(\frac{1}{\delta}\right)+d\log\left(\Big(1+\frac{T}{d\lambda_{0}}\Big)\right)}\;+\;\sqrt{\lambda_{0}}\,S^{\star}, ℰ : \displaystyle\mathcal{E}\;: = { ∥ θ ^ t − θ ⋆ ∥ V t ≤ β for all ​ t ∈ [ T ] } . \displaystyle=\;\Big\{\,\lVert\hat{\theta}_{t}-\theta^{\star}\rVert_{V_{t}}\leq\beta\ \ \text{for all }t\in[T]\,\Big\}. Then ℙ ⁡ ( ℰ ) ≥ 1 − δ \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{E})\geq 1-\delta . The following regret bound holds for all α > 0 \alpha>0 ; the confidence width β \beta and the event ℰ \mathcal{E} are used in the analysis only. Theorem 4.2 ( α \alpha -LinUCB regret) . Let Assumptions (A1) and (A2) hold. On the event ℰ \mathcal{E} , hence with probability at least 1 − δ 1-\delta , ℛ T = 𝒪 ⁡ ( M m ​ α 2 + β 2 α ​ d ​ T ) . \mathcal{R}_{T}\;=\;{\mathcal{O}}\Big(\frac{M}{m}\,\frac{\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2}}{\alpha}\,\sqrt{dT}\Big). Theorem 4.2 shows that α \alpha -LinUCB has sublinear regret for every α > 0 \alpha>0 , including values for which 𝒞 t ​ ( α ) \mathcal{C}_{t}(\alpha) is not a valid confidence set. The bound depends on the geometry of the action set through the ratio M / m M/m , similarly to the bound of Abeille et al. (2025) for randomised exploration algorithms. As α \alpha decreases, the set 𝒞 t ​ ( α ) \mathcal{C}_{t}(\alpha) shrinks towards { θ ^ t } \{\hat{\theta}_{t}\} and the algorithm approaches the greedy policy; accordingly, the guarantee degrades. Likewise, the bound deteriorates as α → ∞ \alpha\to\infty , when the algorithm fails to exploit known information. Optimising the bound over α \alpha gives α = β \alpha=\beta , and one recovers standard LinUCB, but with a regret bound of 𝒪 ⁡ ( ( M / m ) ​ d ​ T ​ log ⁡ ( T ) ) {\mathcal{O}}((M/m)\,d\sqrt{T\log\left(T\right)}) , a log ⁡ ( T ) \sqrt{\log\left(T\right)} improvement over the 𝒪 ⁡ ( d ​ T ​ log ⁡ ( T ) ) \mathcal{O}(d\sqrt{T}\log\left(T\right)) upper bound of Abbasi-Yadkori et al. (2011) . Theorem 4.3 (Spectral Growth) . Let Assumptions (A1) and (A2) hold, let ℰ \mathcal{E} and β \beta be as in Proposition 4.1 , and let T B = 𝒪 ⁡ ( poly ⁡ ( log ⁡ T ) ) T_{B}=\mathcal{O}(\operatorname{poly}(\log T)) be the burn-in threshold. sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: This paper studied the α \alpha -LinUCB family of algorithms for stochastic linear bandits, in which the exploration radius α \alpha is treated as a free parameter rather than as a statistical confidence width. Under a curvature assumption on the action set, we established a sublinear regret bound that holds for every α > 0 \alpha>0 , irrespective of whether 𝒞 t ​ ( α ) \mathcal{C}_{t}(\alpha) is a valid confidence set. The bound rests on a fine-grained analysis of the spectral growth of the design matrix, which shows that α \alpha -LinUCB explores every direction at a rate that we quantify explicitly. This analysis serves two purposes. It substitutes for the optimism inequality, which is no longer guaranteed once θ ⋆ ∉ 𝒞 t ​ ( α ) \theta^{\star}\notin\mathcal{C}_{t}(\alpha) , and thereby extends the guarantee to arbitrary radii; and it circumvents the elliptical potential lemma, thereby improving by a factor log ⁡ ( T ) \sqrt{\log\left(T\right)} the best known regret bound for standard LinUCB. A single factor log ⁡ ( T ) \sqrt{\log\left(T\right)} nonetheless separates our bound from the Ω ⁡ ( d ​ T ) \Omega(d\sqrt{T}) lower bound, and it is now inherited from the concentration inequality for the adaptive design alone. While Lattimore (2023) rules out the removal of this factor in the general adaptive case, it may still be possible to dispense with it within the family of algorithms considered here, now that the dynamics of the algorithm, and the rate at which each direction of the design matrix grows, are better understood. This question is both interesting and far from straightforward, and we leave it for future work.

sections.heading: Reproducibility Statement
sections.text: This work is primarily theoretical. All assumptions required to derive our results are precisely stated and discussed in the main text ( Assumptions (A1) and (A2) ). Proof sketches are provided in the main text, and complete proofs are included in the appendices. The full protocol of the simulations (instance, parameters, number of replications) is specified in Section 7 .

The bound of Abbasi-Yadkori et al. (2011) handles the sequential design through a self-normalised martingale inequality (the method of mixtures): the quantity ∥ ∑ s < t x s ​ η s ∥ V t − 1 \lVert\sum_{s<t}x_{s}\eta_{s}\rVert_{V_{t}^{-1}} is controlled simultaneously for all t t , whatever the dependence of x s x_{s} on the past, at the price of the log det V t ≤ d log ( ( 1 + t / ( d λ 0 ) ) ) \log\det V_{t}\leq d\log\left((1+t/(d\lambda_{0}))\right) term, i.e. of the factor log ⁡ ( T ) \sqrt{\log\left(T\right)} in β ≍ d ​ log ⁡ ( T ) \beta\asymp\sqrt{d\log\left(T\right)} . sections.text: Algorithm 1 summarises the algorithm analysed in this paper; we briefly comment on its steps, complementing the description given in Section 1 . Algorithm 1 α \alpha -LinUCB 1 Input: Action set 𝒳 \mathcal{X} , horizon T T , regularization parameter λ 0 > 0 \lambda_{0}>0 , and exploration radius α > 0 \alpha>0 2 Initialize: V 1 ← λ 0 ​ 𝐈 V_{1}\leftarrow\lambda_{0}\mathbf{I} 3 for t = 1 , … , T t=1,\ldots,T do 4 Compute the ridge estimate θ ^ t \hat{\theta}_{t} ⊳ \triangleright Estimation 5 Select an action–parameter: ( x t , θ t ) ∈ arg ​ max ( x , θ ) ∈ 𝒳 × 𝒞 t ​ ( α ) ⁡ ⟨ x , θ ⟩ (x_{t},\theta_{t})\in\argmax\limits_{(x,\theta)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{C}_{t}(\alpha)}{\langle x,\theta\rangle} ⊳ \triangleright Decision rule 6 Play x t x_{t} and observe the reward y t y_{t} ⊳ \triangleright Feedback 7 Update V t + 1 ← V t + x t ​ x t ⊤ V_{t+1}\leftarrow V_{t}+x_{t}x_{t}^{\top} ⊳ \triangleright Design-matrix update

sections.heading: Estimation (line 1 ).
sections.text: The ridge estimate is θ ^ t = V t − 1 ​ ∑ s = 1 t − 1 x s ​ y s \hat{\theta}_{t}=V_{t}^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}x_{s}y_{s} with design matrix V t = λ 0 ​ 𝐈 + ∑ s = 1 t − 1 x s ​ x s ⊤ V_{t}=\lambda_{0}\mathbf{I}+\sum_{s=1}^{t-1}x_{s}x_{s}^{\top} ; both admit rank-one updates, so each round costs 𝒪 ⁡ ( d 2 ) \mathcal{O}(d^{2}) beyond the decision rule.

sections.heading: Decision rule (line 1 ).
sections.text: The pair ( x t , θ t ) (x_{t},\theta_{t}) maximises ⟨ x , θ ⟩ {\langle x,\theta\rangle} jointly over 𝒳 × 𝒞 t ​ ( α ) \mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{C}_{t}(\alpha) , where 𝒞 t ​ ( α ) = { θ : ∥ θ − θ ^ t ∥ V t ≤ α } \mathcal{C}_{t}(\alpha)=\{\theta:\lVert\theta-\hat{\theta}_{t}\rVert_{V_{t}}\leq\alpha\} . Optimising first over θ \theta at fixed x x gives the equivalent bonus form x t ∈ arg ​ max x ∈ 𝒳 ⁡ { ⟨ θ ^ t , x ⟩ + α ​ ∥ x ∥ V t − 1 } , x_{t}\in\argmax_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\Big\{{\langle\hat{\theta}_{t},x\rangle}+\alpha\lVert x\rVert_{V_{t}^{-1}}\Big\}, the familiar upper-confidence-bound rule, with ∥ x ∥ V t − 1 \lVert x\rVert_{V_{t}^{-1}} largest along the directions least represented in the design; conversely, once x t x_{t} is chosen, θ t = θ ^ t + α ​ V t − 1 ​ x t / ∥ x t ∥ V t − 1 \theta_{t}=\hat{\theta}_{t}+\alpha V_{t}^{-1}x_{t}/\lVert x_{t}\rVert_{V_{t}^{-1}} attains the inner maximum.

sections.heading: The radius α \alpha .
sections.text: The only departure from standard LinUCB is that the radius α \alpha is an arbitrary input, held fixed over the run, rather than the concentration width β \beta of Proposition 4.1 : for α = β \alpha=\beta the algorithm is exactly the optimistic algorithm of Abbasi-Yadkori et al. (2011) , while for α < β \alpha<\beta the set 𝒞 t ​ ( α ) \mathcal{C}_{t}(\alpha) need not contain θ ⋆ \theta^{\star} at any round, and as α → 0 \alpha\to 0 the rule approaches the greedy policy. Neither β \beta nor any property of the noise beyond the observations themselves is used by the algorithm; they appear in the analysis only.

sections.text: The engine equation 22 is a lower bound on x t ⊤ ​ V t − 1 ​ x t x_{t}^{\top}V_{t}^{-1}x_{t} , while the crude bound equation 30 is an upper bound on the sum of these quantities. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2611.04641v1 [cs.LG] 03 Nov 2026 Does LinUCB Need Valid Confidence Sets? Ahmed Ben Yahmed † † thanks: Correspondence to: a.benyahmed@criteo.com. Affiliation: Criteo AI Lab, Paris, France Affiliation: CREST, ENSAE, Institut Polytechnique de Paris, France Affiliation: FairPlay joint team, Inria, France Marc Abeille Affiliation: Criteo AI Lab, Paris, France Affiliation: FairPlay joint team, Inria, France David Janz & Clément Calauzènes Affiliation: Criteo AI Lab, Paris, France Affiliation: FairPlay joint team, Inria, France Affiliation: University of Oxford Abstract We show that replacing LinUCB’s usual confidence width β  eta by any fixed α > 0 \alpha>0 preserves sublinear regret when the action set is M M -smooth and m m -strongly convex. Our high-probability regret bound for this generalisation, α \alpha -LinUCB, establishes that valid confidence sets are not necessary for the success of LinUCB. We identify the mechanism behind this result: action-set curvature drives α \alpha -LinUCB to explore every direction, even when optimism is not guaranteed. To analyse this mechanism, we introduce a logarithmically capped spectral potential that, unlike the standard log-determinant potential, caps contributions from well-explored directions. This yields lower bounds on the smallest eigenvalue of the design matrix. We discuss these and further connections below. Optimism and confidence sets in linear bandits. The classical 𝒪 ⁡ ( d ​ T ​ log ⁡ ( T ) ) \mathcal{O}(d\sqrt{T}\log\left(Tight)) regret analysis of LinUCB/OFUL combines self-normalised concentration with the elliptical-potential lemma ( Li et al., 2010 ; Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2011 ) . Each contributes a log ⁡ ( T ) \sqrt{\log\left(Tight)} factor, leaving a logarithmic gap to the Ω ⁡ ( d ​ T ) \Omega(d\sqrt{T}) minimax lower bound ( Dani et al., 2008 ; Rusmevichientong & Tsitsiklis, 2010 ; Lattimore & Szepesvári, 2020 ) . Lattimore (2023) proves that the continuous-time counterpart of the self-normalised concentration bound cannot be improved for general adaptive covariates. Flynn et al. (2023) construct tighter confidence sequences using adaptive martingale mixtures, improving empirical performance while retaining 𝒪 ⁡ ( d ​ T ​ log ⁡ ( T ) ) \mathcal{O}(d\sqrt{T}\log\left(Tight)) worst-case regret. Our analysis uses the standard confidence bound but with a logarithmically capped potential. Classical frequentist analyses of linear Thompson sampling also rely on optimism: posterior inflation ensures a constant probability of an optimistic draw, at the cost of an additional d \sqrt{d} factor in the regret bound ( Agrawal & Goyal, 2013 ; Abeille & Lazaric, 2017 ) . For finite-armed linear bandits, Lattimore & Szepesvári (2017) show that standard optimism-based algorithms can be suboptimal. Subsequent asymptotically optimal algorithms explicitly optimise exploration allocations to account for the information provided by suboptimal actions ( Hao et al., 2020 ; Tirinzoni et al., 2020 ) . Conditions on the growth of the design matrix play a central role in inference from adaptively collected data, beginning with Lai & Wei (1982) .
